stem: A researcher surveyed $500$ voters selected at random from the list of all registered voters in a city. To which group can the results of the survey most appropriately be generalized?
choices: All registered voters in the city
All registered voters in the country
Only the $500$ voters who were surveyed
All residents of the city, including those who are not registered voters
explanation:
Results from a random sample apply to the group the sample was drawn from, and no further.

These $500$ voters were picked at random from the list of registered voters in this city. So the results can be extended to all registered voters in the city.

Ask yourself two questions on these problems: who could have been picked, and were they picked at random?

rationales.B: Voters outside the city had no chance to be picked, so the sample says nothing reliable about them.
rationales.C: Because the sample was random, it represents more than just the $500$ people asked. It speaks for the whole list it was drawn from.
rationales.D: Only registered voters could be picked. People who aren't registered weren't part of the group sampled.

stem: An observational study of high school students found that students who eat breakfast every day tend to have higher test scores than students who do not. Which conclusion is best supported by the study?
choices: Eating breakfast every day causes students to earn higher test scores.
Among the students studied, eating breakfast every day is associated with higher test scores.
Requiring students to eat breakfast would raise their test scores.
Skipping breakfast causes students to earn lower test scores.
explanation:
In an observational study, researchers just watch what people already do. They don't decide who eats breakfast.

That means the breakfast eaters might differ in other ways too, like sleep, routines, or support at home. Any of those could explain the higher scores.

So the study can show that breakfast and scores go together (an association), but not that breakfast causes the higher scores.

To show cause and effect, researchers need to randomly assign who gets the treatment.

rationales.A: Nobody was assigned to eat breakfast, so other differences between the groups could explain the scores. That rules out claiming a cause.
rationales.C: This predicts what would happen if breakfast were required, but the study never tried that. It only observed students.
rationales.D: This is still a cause and effect claim, just flipped around. An observational study can't support it.

stem: In an experiment, $60$ tomato plants were randomly assigned to receive a new fertilizer and $60$ were randomly assigned to receive no fertilizer. The mean growth was $14.8$ centimeters for the fertilizer group and $11.3$ centimeters for the other group. How many centimeters greater was the mean growth of the fertilizer group?
explanation:
"How much greater" asks for a difference, so subtract the two means.

$14.8 - 11.3 = 3.5$ centimeters.

Because the plants were randomly assigned, this difference can fairly be credited to the fertilizer.

stem: A teacher wants to test whether using a new vocabulary app improves students' vocabulary scores. Which study design would best allow the teacher to conclude that the app causes an improvement?
choices: Let students decide whether to use the app, then compare the scores of users and non-users.
Give the app to all students this year and compare their scores with last year's students.
Randomly assign students from a large group to either use the app or not, then compare the two groups' scores.
Survey students who already use the app about whether their scores have improved.
explanation:
To show that the app causes better scores, the only real difference between the two groups should be the app.

Randomly assigning students to use it or not does that. With a large group, random assignment spreads things like motivation and ability evenly across both groups. If the app group then scores higher, the app is the best explanation.

The other designs let some other difference sneak in.

rationales.A: Students who choose the app might already be more motivated, so the groups differ in more than just the app.
rationales.B: This year's class and last year's class can differ in many ways, so you can't tell if the app made the difference.
rationales.D: Asking current users how they feel has no comparison group, and people's opinions of their own progress can be biased.

stem: A researcher selected $200$ adults at random from the members of a city's gyms. Half were randomly assigned to follow a high-protein diet and half to follow their usual diet. After $12$ weeks, the high-protein group had gained significantly more muscle. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
choices: A high-protein diet causes greater muscle gain for adults in the city.
A high-protein diet causes greater muscle gain for adults in the country.
No conclusion about cause and effect can be drawn because only $200$ adults were studied.
A high-protein diet likely causes greater muscle gain for members of the city's gyms.
explanation:
Two separate questions decide what you can conclude.

Can you claim cause and effect? Yes, because the diets were randomly assigned.

Who does it apply to? Only the group the people were randomly selected from: members of this city's gyms.

Put together: a high protein diet likely causes more muscle gain for members of the city's gyms.

rationales.A: Everyone in the study came from gym members, who may differ from adults who don't go to a gym. The result can't stretch that far.
rationales.B: The sample came from one city's gyms, so it can't speak for the whole country.
rationales.C: Random assignment, not a huge sample, is what allows a cause and effect claim. $200$ people randomly assigned is enough.

stem: A student council surveyed $80$ randomly selected students about a proposed later start time, and $32$ of them said they support it. A council member claims that most students support the proposal. What percent of the surveyed students supported the proposal?
explanation:
Percent of the sample that supports it: $\frac{32}{80} = 0.40$, or 40%.

Notice what this means for the council member's claim. "Most" means more than half, but only 40% of the sample said yes. The survey doesn't back up the claim.

stem: A survey of $1{,}000$ adults selected at random from a region found that adults who own a dog reported exercising more minutes per week, on average, than adults who do not own a dog. Which statement is best supported by the survey?
choices: Among adults in the region, owning a dog is associated with reporting more exercise.
Owning a dog causes adults in the region to exercise more.
The association applies only to the $1{,}000$ adults who were surveyed.
If an adult in the region gets a dog, that adult will exercise more.
explanation:
Again, two questions.

Who does it apply to? The adults were randomly selected from the region, so the result applies to adults in the region.

Is it cause and effect? No. Nobody was assigned a dog; people already owned one or didn't. People who love exercise might be more likely to get a dog in the first place.

So the best conclusion is an association among adults in the region.

rationales.B: Dog ownership wasn't assigned. Active people may simply be more likely to own dogs, so you can't say the dog causes the exercise.
rationales.C: Because the adults were chosen at random from the region, the association can be extended to the region's adults.
rationales.D: This predicts that getting a dog would change one person's habits. That is a cause and effect claim the survey can't support.

stem: A local news website asked its visitors to vote on whether the city should build a new stadium. Of the $5{,}000$ visitors who voted, 78% voted yes. Which of the following is the best reason the result may not represent the opinion of the city's residents?
choices: A sample of $5{,}000$ is too small to represent a city.
78% is too high a percent to be accurate.
The voters chose to respond, and many of them may not live in the city.
A margin of error cannot be found for a percent.
explanation:
The problem is how the sample was chosen. Visitors decided for themselves whether to vote. People with strong feelings are much more likely to bother, and anyone online could vote, including people who don't live in the city.

That makes it a voluntary response sample, which may not match the city's residents, no matter how many people vote.

A large sample can't fix a biased way of choosing it.

rationales.A: $5{,}000$ is a large sample. The trouble is that it wasn't random, not that it's too small.
rationales.B: A high percent isn't a sign of bias by itself. Sometimes most people really do agree.
rationales.D: Margins of error are reported for percents all the time. The real issue is that the sample wasn't random.

stem: In a randomized experiment, $150$ participants were assigned to take a new sleep aid and $150$ were assigned to take a placebo. In the sleep-aid group, $96$ participants reported improved sleep; in the placebo group, $66$ did. By how many percentage points was the percent reporting improved sleep in the sleep-aid group greater than in the placebo group?
explanation:
Turn each group's count into a percent so the groups can be compared fairly.

Sleep aid: $\frac{96}{150} = 0.64$, which is 64%.

Placebo: $\frac{66}{150} = 0.44$, which is 44%.

The difference is $64 - 44 = 20$ percentage points.
